claims.text: A business objective is a target a business sets itself to reach within a defined period, such as a year; examples include surviving the first year of trading or reaching a profit of N$200 000.

verification.method: Authored originally against the 0450 v2 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires independent semantic review (RS-28) before publication.

claims.text: Objectives give a business direction: decisions about spending, pricing and where to sell can each be tested against the stated target, which guides everyday choices instead of habit.

verification.method: Authored originally against the 0450 v2 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires independent semantic review (RS-28) before publication.

claims.text: Objectives matter because they let a business measure progress against a target and act when results fall short, coordinate its teams around one stated aim, and give the workforce something concrete to reach.

verification.method: Authored originally against the 0450 v2 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires independent semantic review (RS-28) before publication.

claims.text: Business objectives change with circumstances: a new business is likely to put survival first, an established one usually pursues profit, growth or market share, and a business whose sales fall may return to survival; several objectives are commonly held at once and can pull against each other.

verification.method: Authored originally against the 0450 v2 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires independent semantic review (RS-28) before publication.

claims.text: Survival means the business keeps trading; new businesses put it first and established businesses return to it when sales fall, because a business that stops trading cannot meet any other objective. In a survival year the watch on cash-flow matters more than the size of profit - the two are not the same, and a business can keep trading while profit is thin.

verification.method: Authored originally against the 0450 v2 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires independent semantic review (RS-28) before publication.

claims.text: Profit is revenue less total costs over a period. It is the return owners receive for the risk they take, and it funds the business's next stage of development.

verification.method: Authored originally against the 0450 v2 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires independent semantic review (RS-28) before publication.

claims.text: Growth means the business becomes larger - more sales, more branches or more products. Growth is internal when the business expands from its own resources, such as a taxi firm adding vehicles, and external when it joins with another business, such as a lodge buying a rival.

verification.method: Authored originally against the 0450 v2 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires independent semantic review (RS-28) before publication.

claims.text: Market share is the proportion of the market's total sales made by one business, usually expressed as a percentage. "The market" here means the customers, actual and potential, for the product - not a physical place.

verification.method: Authored originally against the 0450 v2 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires independent semantic review (RS-28) before publication.

claims.text: A social enterprise is a business with social aims that uses business activity - producing and selling goods or services - to achieve them, funding its work mainly by trading rather than by donations.

verification.method: Authored originally against the 0450 v2 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires independent semantic review (RS-28) before publication.

claims.text: A social enterprise typically pursues objectives on three fronts together: social objectives that help people or a community, environmental objectives that protect the natural world, and financial objectives that keep the business itself sound, because a social enterprise that runs out of money stops helping anyone.

verification.method: Authored originally against the 0450 v2 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires independent semantic review (RS-28) before publication.

claims.text: For a social enterprise, profit is usually a means to keep the social aim running rather than the main aim, and decisions often trade the two against each other - a bigger surplus can mean a better-funded mission or a thinner one.

verification.method: Authored originally against the 0450 v2 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires independent semantic review (RS-28) before publication.

claims.text: A stakeholder is any person or group with an interest in what a business does - anyone affected by its decisions, for better or worse.

verification.method: Authored originally against the 0450 v2 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires independent semantic review (RS-28) before publication.

claims.text: Internal stakeholder groups are the workers, managers and owners inside the business; external stakeholder groups include customers, suppliers, lenders, government and the local community, who hold their interest from outside.

verification.method: Authored originally against the 0450 v2 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires independent semantic review (RS-28) before publication.

claims.text: The boundary between internal and external stakeholders is employment and ownership: people the business employs or who own it are internal, while those whose link is a purchase, a contract or an address are external.

verification.method: Authored originally against the 0450 v2 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires independent semantic review (RS-28) before publication.

claims.text: Internal stakeholders' objectives follow from their position: workers want fair pay, safe conditions and job security; managers add career progress and the results their salary is judged on; owners want profit and growth in what the business is worth.

verification.method: Authored originally against the 0450 v2 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires independent semantic review (RS-28) before publication.

claims.text: External stakeholders' objectives follow from their own interest: customers want quality at a fair price and reliable supply; suppliers want prompt payment and repeat orders; lenders want repayment with interest; government wants tax revenue, jobs and legal behaviour; the community wants local jobs without pollution.

verification.method: Authored originally against the 0450 v2 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires independent semantic review (RS-28) before publication.

claims.text: Because each group's interest differs, one business decision typically helps some stakeholder groups and works against others, so managers have to weigh the effects on each group rather than treat stakeholders as one.

verification.method: Authored originally against the 0450 v2 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires independent semantic review (RS-28) before publication.

claims.text: A stakeholder conflict is a situation in which the objectives of two or more stakeholder groups cannot all be fully met by one decision, such as owners seeking profit while workers seek a wage rise that would absorb most of it.

verification.method: Authored originally against the 0450 v2 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires independent semantic review (RS-28) before publication.

claims.text: Typical stakeholder conflicts include owners wanting low wages to protect profit against workers wanting higher pay, and customers wanting lower prices against owners wanting a higher margin on each sale.

verification.method: Authored originally against the 0450 v2 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires independent semantic review (RS-28) before publication.

claims.text: Because stakeholder objectives trade off against each other, businesses usually settle conflicts by compromise - a staged wage rise, a smaller price increase - ranking groups by how much the business depends on them; no decision satisfies every group in full.

verification.method: Authored originally against the 0450 v2 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires independent semantic review (RS-28) before publication.

claims.text: Private sector enterprises are owned by individuals or shareholders, while public sector enterprises are owned and controlled by central or local government, which is answerable to the public for the services they provide.

verification.method: Authored originally against the 0450 v2 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires independent semantic review (RS-28) before publication.

claims.text: Private businesses are led by profit, survival and growth, while public sector enterprises pursue service objectives - access for users a private firm might find unprofitable to serve, affordability, reliability - and aim to cover costs rather than maximise profit.

verification.method: Authored originally against the 0450 v2 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires independent semantic review (RS-28) before publication.

claims.text: Ownership drives the difference in objectives: the group that owns an enterprise sets what success means for it, so a state-owned utility is judged on service while a family-owned firm is judged on the return it earns.

verification.method: Authored originally against the 0450 v2 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires independent semantic review (RS-28) before publication.
